sections.h2: Who bills and who values property in Clayton County?
sections.html:
Two separate Clayton County offices touch every parcel. The Board of Tax Assessors sets the value, and the Tax Commissioner mails the bill, collects the money and passes it on to the county, the cities, fire services and the school board. Neither one sets the millage rate. That job belongs to the county commissioners, and the school board and each city set their own rates for their own bills.

Both offices work out of the county government complex in Jonesboro, at 121 South McDonough Street. The assessors sit in Annex 3 on the 4th floor and can be reached at (770) 477-3285. The Tax Commissioner is in Annex 3 on the 2nd floor, with a property tax line at (770) 477-3311. Knowing which door to knock on saves a seller days, because a value question sent to the commissioner or a payoff question sent to the assessors simply gets redirected.

The assessors value property as of January 1. A house you sell in October is still billed on the January 1 owner record, which is why the tax bill and the closing statement need to be read together when you sell a house in Clayton County.

sections.h2: What is Clayton County like for someone selling a house?
sections.html:
Clayton County is a compact, heavily built-up county south of Atlanta. It covers 144 square miles, which makes it the third smallest county in Georgia by area. Jonesboro is the county seat, Forest Park is the largest city, and Clayton State University sits in Morrow. The county also holds most of Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport.

The 2020 census counted 297,595 residents, 106,200 households and 114,038 housing units, with 6.9% of those units vacant. Owners and renters are nearly even: 49.5% of occupied homes were owner-occupied and 50.5% were rented. The median age was 34.3. With half the occupied homes rented, a seller with a tenant in place has plenty of company, and a lease is one more thing to settle before a closing date.

The county sits across two river basins, with the eastern side between Forest Park and Lovejoy draining toward the Ocmulgee and the western side toward the Flint. Interstates 75, 85, 285 and 675 all cross it, along with US 19/41 (Tara Boulevard) and State Routes 54, 85 and 138. Conley and Irondale are census-designated places, and Ellenwood, Rex and Mountain View are unincorporated communities. Ask the Tax Commissioner whether your parcel also carries a city bill.

sections.h2: When are Clayton County property tax bills due?
sections.html:
The Tax Commissioner's own presentation describes a yearly rhythm. Assessment notices go out in spring or early summer, the millage rate process runs from about mid July to mid August, and bills follow around mid September, with a due date usually in mid November. Owners get 60 days from the mail-out to pay. The exact mail-out and due dates change from year to year, so check the bill itself or call (770) 477-3311.

If your value is under appeal when bills go out, you receive two bills. The first is for 85% of the amount and is due on the regular due date. The second covers the remaining 15%, and it is due, or refunded, after the appeal settles. The bill itself is the only place the exact amounts appear, so ask for a copy before you list the house.

Georgia's revenue department adds a few statewide rules that apply here too. Interest does not start until 60 days after the postmark on the bill. Delinquent balances can also pick up penalties. A refund claim for tax that was wrongly assessed must start within three years of payment, and a refund tied to an appeal is processed once the final value is set.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Clayton County property assessment?
sections.html:
You have 45 days from the date printed on the notice of assessment, and the appeal must be in writing. The same 45-day window covers applying for a homestead exemption from the notice. Miss it and the right to appeal that year's value is lost. Appeals are filed with the Board of Tax Assessors at the Annex 3 office, and the county also runs an online appeals portal for them.

The notice itself lists four routes after the first review. The table below summarizes what the county prints on its assessment notice.

Appeal routes listed on the Clayton County notice of assessment (Clayton County Board of Tax Assessors)
RouteWhat it can decideCondition printed on the notice
Board of EqualizationValue, uniformity, exemptions or taxabilityOpen to any owner who files in time
Nonbinding arbitrationValue onlyRequires a certified appraisal
Hearing officerValue or uniformityNon-homestead real property worth more than $500,000, or certain business personal property accounts above the listed totals
Superior CourtAs agreedRequires a written agreement with the Board of Tax Assessors

The assessors must hand over the records they used to set your value within 10 business days of a request. Ask for them early. Sales of similar houses nearby and photos of problems the county could not see from the street are the usual evidence. An appeal can challenge value, uniformity or taxability. It cannot challenge the tax rate.

sections.h2: Which exemptions can a Clayton County homeowner claim?
sections.html:
Homestead exemptions apply only to the home you own and live in as your primary residence on January 1, and you can hold only one. The Tax Commissioner takes the applications. The statewide filing season runs from January 1 to April 1, and the county says it accepts applications all year, though a late filing waits for the next tax year. Once the exemption is granted it renews each year, and you must tell the office if you stop qualifying.

A local base-year homestead measure was prepared for Clayton voters on the November 4, 2025 ballot. As the commissioner's office described it, the measure would freeze the county-purposes value for senior residents age 65 or older, disabled veterans, surviving spouses of peace officers or firefighters killed in the line of duty, and 100 percent disabled residents, for tax years 2026 through 2030. Ask the Tax Commissioner whether it applies to your parcel and how it appears on your bill.

If you sell, the exemption belongs to your residence status and not to the house. A buyer applies on their own once they own and occupy it, so a seller should not expect the exemption to carry over, and the buyer's first bill may be higher than yours was.

sections.h2: What happens if taxes go unpaid on a Clayton County house?
sections.html:
Unpaid taxes lead to an execution on the property and, eventually, a tax sale. The Tax Commissioner's property portal links to tax sale notices for the October 2026 and November 2026 sales, a bidder pre-registration form, and an excess funds claim form for owners owed money after a sale. Those links show how active the process is in a county this size.

A tax sale transfers a tax deed and not clear title, and Georgia law gives the owner a right to redeem. Even so, a house with a tax lien is hard to finance or insure. A buyer using a mortgage will want the taxes paid, and a closing office will ask for the delinquent balance to be cleared from proceeds. If you have fallen behind, call (770) 477-3311 before you list the house, and ask for the total needed to clear the account on a specific closing date.

sections.h2: How are property taxes handled when you sell in Clayton County?
sections.html:
Georgia does not run tax proration through the county. Taxes are billed to the owner of record on January 1, and the closing attorney or title company decides who pays what share in the sales contract and on the settlement statement. Ask the closing office to order a tax certificate or payoff so the bill and any city bill are paid from proceeds at closing.

  • Pull your current bill from the Tax Commissioner's portal and note whether a city bill also applies.
  • Ask whether an appeal is pending, because a pending appeal means a second bill for the remaining 15%.
  • Confirm any homestead exemption will be removed after the sale.
  • Keep the closing statement. It is your record that the bill was paid.

If the taxes, a repair list and a tenant are all complicating a Clayton County sale, a cash buyer who buys as-is can close without waiting for a lender's appraisal and inspection. Ask for any offer in writing and compare it with what an agent sale would net after repairs.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Clayton County assessment?
faqs.a: You have 45 days from the date printed on the notice of assessment, and the appeal must be in writing. File with the Board of Tax Assessors at 121 S. McDonough Street, Annex 3, 4th floor in Jonesboro, or use the county's online appeals portal. A missed deadline means the value stands for that year.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a Clayton County tax bill?
faqs.a: Call the Tax Commissioner's property tax line at (770) 477-3311 for bills, payments, exemptions and payoffs. Call the Board of Tax Assessors at (770) 477-3285 for value, notices and appeals. The assessors do not collect money, and the commissioner does not change values.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay while my Clayton County appeal is pending?
faqs.a: Yes, in part. A property under appeal gets two bills. The first, for 85% of the amount, is due on the normal due date. The remaining 15% is due, or refunded, once the appeal is decided, so a settled appeal can produce either a small balance or a refund.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Clayton County house if the property taxes are unpaid?
faqs.a: Yes. The closing attorney or title company pays the back taxes from your proceeds at closing, so you need a payoff figure for the closing date. If a tax sale has already happened, the buyer of the tax deed holds a lien-like interest until the owner redeems, which adds a step. Call (770) 477-3311 first.

faqs.q: Does my homestead exemption go to the next owner of my Clayton County house?
faqs.a: No. A homestead exemption attaches to the person who owns and lives in the home as a primary residence on January 1. The buyer must file their own application with the Tax Commissioner. The commissioner takes applications from January through April 1 and will process late ones for the following year.
